records.title: Age-of-acquisition Effects across the Adult Lifespan: Evidence from Eye Movements in Compound Word Reading
records.summary: The Age of Acquisition (AoA) effect is where words acquired during childhood are recognised more quickly than those acquired during adulthood. However, the influence of AoA on compound words and its stability across the adult lifespan remain under-investigated. We conducted two eye-tracking experiments to clarify how the AoA effect is moderated by ageing and spacing. Ninety British English adults participated across two eye-tracking experiments: 60 young adults (30 reading unspaced compounds in Experiment 1 and 30 reading spaced compounds in Experiment 2) and 30 older adults (who read both unspaced and spaced compounds across experiments). records.title: Development and psychometric properties of the CDI-IIIR for language assessment of 30- to 48-month-olds
records.summary: The Macarthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDI) are a set of widely used parent-report instruments for measuring young children’s language development. The most widely used measures for English-speaking children are the CDIs for 8-30 months. There is a strong need for both clinical and research purpose for comparable measures for three-year-olds. The previously published U.S. English CDI-III yielded norms for 30-37 months only, due to ceiling effects, and assessed limited aspects of language. Recent adaptations for Swedish and other Scandinavian languages, have used a different design and showed strong psychometric properties for children 2.5-4 years old. The current study …

records.title: Examining Biliteracy and Bidirectional Cross-Linguistic Transfer in a Low Literacy and Multilingual Context: Insights from Internally Displaced Children in Northeast Nigeria
records.summary: Internally-displaced children often lack schooling and reside in highly multilingual contexts. In Nigeria, children must learn to read in a local language (e.g., Hausa), and English; here, language skills can transfer across languages to support biliteracy. Importantly, the strength of transfer is constrained by proficiency in language skills. Formal schooling and early life exposure are crucial for acquisition of language skills. records.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ): Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
records.summary: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). records.title: Consensus-based TRansparent, sUStainable, and Transferable (TRUST) best-practice guidelines for visual word recognition research
records.summary: Reading is a fundamental life skill, and at its basis is the ability to process single words. Researchers often study single-word processing using lexical decision tasks. However, most research is conducted in a single language by separate research groups, limiting comparability, replicability, and generalizability. In addition, best-practice knowledge is often only transmitted informally within labs, leading to heterogeneity and reduced reproducibility across labs. Here, we, the TRUST Consortium, established a consensus-based research guideline for current best practices in psycholinguistic reading research by integrating expert knowledge. records.title: How much data? Measuring the complexity of thematic coding tasks and the amount of training samples needed for supervised modeling
records.summary: Traditional methods of thematic analysis are critical for deep, nuanced understanding of complex planning challenges, but the manual intensity of the process limits its applications to increasingly large datasets generated by planning processes. Hybrid, supervised methods of natural language processing offer a solution by allowing researchers to scale theory-driven topics by using traditional methods to first label a sample of the data. However, because the amount of labeled data needed varies across thematic analysis tasks, researchers and practitioners face uncertainty in the time, cost, and feasibility of applying scalable text analysis to planning research and practice. records.summary: Research on linguistic illusions has debated what information is used to access memory representations, but how speakers use surface phonological information during dependency resolution remains unclear. Agreement attraction is more likely when the attractor matches the form of an agreement controller (e.g., in case marking). This has been attributed to phonological forms directly activating every feature set they can express, regardless of context. Alternatively, form may act indirectly, by shifting the estimated probability that a noun is a controller, which retrieval uses as a cue. records.title: The Impact of Attention on Speech Entrainment in Clinical High-Risk for Psychosis Individuals
records.summary: Language comprehension is disrupted in schizophrenia and early-stage psychosis, but the contributions of bottom-up and top-down processing remain unclear. In the current electroencephalography (EEG) study, we investigated speech entrainment in a sample of n=21 individuals at clinical high-risk for psychosis (CHR-P) and n=25 healthy controls (HCs). records.title: PraBat: An item response theory-based test battery to assess individual differences in pragmatic abilities in preschool children from different cultural backgrounds
records.summary: Pragmatic abilities allow us to use and comprehend language in interaction. The assessment of individual differences in pragmatic abilities, both within and across cultural settings, is crucial to understanding how they develop. However, tools with good psychometric properties that suit this purpose are lacking. The current study describes the creation of a test battery assessing individual differences in 3- to 6-year-old children from different cultural and linguistic backgrounds. The battery is implemented as a tablet-based game, administrable both online and in person. records.title: The dimensionality and influence of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in Nordfriesland and Fryslân
records.summary: This study examined parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism in the district of Nordfriesland, Germany, and the province of Fryslân, the Netherlands. Both are home to speakers of the local majority language (i.e. German/Dutch), autochthonous heritage languages (e.g. Frisian), and immigrant heritage languages (e.g. Arabic). Quantitative questionnaire data were collected from 645 parents of young children, making this the first large-scale study of parental attitudes towards childhood multilingualism outside Québec. records.title: Beyond Behavioral Adaptation: Evaluating the Added Value of EEG in Personalized Language Interfaces
records.summary: Neuroadaptive interfaces personalize human–computer interaction using brain activity, but whether neural measurements provide useful information beyond behavioral indicators remains unclear, particularly in language comprehension tasks. We propose a framework to investigate the added value of EEG in adaptive communication support. Written messages are presented through combinations of sentence segmentation, pictograms, and keyword labels, with presentation choices informed by individual preferences and task performance. records.title: Musical Genes: A Conceptual Framework for Culturally Informed Feature Extraction in Traditional Music
records.summary: Feature extraction in traditional music requires decisions about which relations to compare, which variations preserve the identity of an analytical unit, and what cultural interpretations the resulting features can support. Drawing on culturally situated information modeling and cross-cultural similarity research, this article develops a conceptual framework through conceptual analysis, a purposive synthesis of the literature, and qualitative reanalysis of selected score excerpts. The term ‘musical gene’ connects two claims about the same candidate unit: that it retains its structural identity across realizations and that it is transmitted through cultural practice. records.title: The Map Is Not the Territory: Construct Names, Items, and Responses in Measures of Mentalizing, Epistemic Trust, and Emotion Regulation
records.summary: Psychology has a measurement problem: different constructs often share the same name, and the same construct is measured under different names. This matters most for constructs theorized as interdependent. In theory, these constructs are defined by name, and their interdependence is posited at that level; in practice, each is measured by a pool of items, often from separate questionnaires, which may overlap or diverge in ways the names do not anticipate. We asked whether construct names correspond to the items that operationalize them, whether items reflect the structure of responses, and whether responses follow the boundaries posited by names or drawn by items. records.title: A set of dynamical rules for conversational progression act as a precursor to collective cognition
records.summary: Conversation unfolds between speakers as a series of coordinated updates from prior ideas expressed in earlier utterances to new sets of ideas. This process of speakers and conversation partners jointly updating prior "conversation states" is an important piece of the cognitive scaffolding that enables social coordination, and even collective cognition -- the capacity for individuals to pool their cognitive resources to solve problems together. However, a functional data-driven description of how this process works is missing in the extant literature. records.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: evidence from infixation and reduplication
records.summary: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped). records.title: Conventionality and transparency in human language
records.summary: The most distinctive feature of language is perhaps the ability to produce and comprehend utterances that have never been said before. This requires language to be transparent: comprehenders can infer the meaning of an utterance based on its components and the rules used to combine them. However, arbitrary associations between form and meaning (conventionality) are ubiquitous in language, despite them being difficult to learn. This is true for words, but also for many utterances. Why is this the case? In this paper, we propose languages balance conventionality and transparency by minimizing the communication and learning cost. records.title: Speech Monitoring During Self-Comprehension
records.summary: Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. records.title: Developmental Changes in Infants’ Ability to Cope with Dialect Variation in Word Segmentation
records.summary: Towards the end of their first year of life, infants learn to ignore variation in sounds not present, or not functional, in their ambient language. Specifically, overly specified word representations are thought to give way to others with which learners can cope better with indexical variation, such as voice and affect, which are not relevant to word identity. This developmental change may help infants in their second year to more efficiently process the ambient language and thus make rapid gains in vocabulary. records.summary: Touch cues might facilitate infants’ early word comprehension and explain why body part words emerge so early. Parents were instructed to teach their infants, 4- to 5-month-olds or 10- to 11-month-olds, nonce words for body parts and a contrast object but were given no instructions about the use of touch. Parents spontaneously touched target body parts in close timing to uttering the target nonce words. They did not show this alignment for unrelated touches and nonce words. records.title: Neural correlates of infant dialect discrimination: An fNIRS study.
records.summary: The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

records.title: A novel method for detecting the onset of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking
records.summary: Determining the onset of experimental effects in timeseries data is central to psycholinguistics, because onset timing constrains theories about when different types of linguistic information become available during language processing. Several onset detection methods have been proposed for the visual world paradigm. An increasingly adopted approach is the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021), but its accuracy in recovering underlying onset values has not yet been formally evaluated. records.title: When edges are not enough: Language-specific distributional regularities shape affix activation
records.summary: Previous experiments have found that an early stage of visual word recognition involves a form-based decomposition process, where morphologically complex words like teacher are broken down into morphemes {teach}+{-er}. However, recent models propose that this decomposition is constrained by edge-alignment—only stems and affixes at word edges are subject to decomposition and subsequent activation. records.title: Multi-Dimensional Reading Anxiety in Adolescence
records.summary: With the global decline in adolescents’ reading skills over the decade, reading-related anxiety begins to draw increasing attention. Over time, the potential feedback loop of higher anxiety and poorer reading may block pathways to academic achievements and increase the likelihood of health problems. This study examined multi-dimensional nature of reading anxiety using a sample of 654 Finnish students in Grades 7-9. The students self-assessed reading anxiety, reading control and values (utility, interest, and importance values), and reading frequency of traditional texts (e.g., book, magazine, newspaper) and digital texts (e.g., social media contents). records.title: Language-Based Mental Health Assessments Do Not Perform Evenly Across Racial and Ethnic Groups
records.summary: Psycholinguistic tools that estimate psychological symptoms from language alone aim to provide unobtrusive assessments without needing questionnaires or clinicians. Researchers largely assume that these assessments function equivalently across demographic groups. We tested this assumption in a racially diverse sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, White) who described their mental health and completed standard symptom questionnaires. records.title: Task effects on predictive eye-movements
records.summary: Research on predictive processing has shown that listeners anticipate upcoming linguistic information using linguistic cues, such as verb meaning. Beyond information in the input, listeners’ prediction can also be influenced by top-down control, such as goals and strategies developed in response to a given task. However, it is unclear to what extent evaluations of task relevance modulate top-down control of prediction. records.title: Gestural relativity of spatial cognition: Gesture can express and transmit the spatial frames of reference that structure thinking
records.summary: When people think spatially, they adopt a frame of reference (egocentric or allocentric). People within a community often rely on the same frame of reference, but there is considerable variation between communities. How are these norms of spatial thinking transmitted? Linguistic relativity posits that they are transmitted through language; evidence for this account is mixed. We investigate a complementary mechanism, gestural relativity, whereby norms of spatial thinking are transmitted by gestures that express spatial information. records.title: Sensitivity to Prosody at 6 Months Predicts Vocabulary at 24 Months
records.summary: Children’s language acquisition appears effortless, and advances enormously between the first word period, at about 12 months, to the stage at which complete and often complex sentences are produced, at about 3 years. However, this apparently miraculous process may in fact rely on knowledge that the child has began to accumulate even before birth. Indeed, work on infant speech perception in the last 40 years suggests that infants begin to attune to their native language during the first year of life.

records.title: Modeling Word Counts: Common Practice Risks False Positives
records.summary: Word counts or relative frequencies (e.g. the number of self-related words as a proportion of total words in a text) are routinely analyzed as dependent variables in the behavioral sciences. We demonstrate that conventional methods of analyzing word counts in this way are likely to lead to false positives, especially when text length varies between levels of the predictor variable. records.title: The design, measurement, and analysis of longitudinal learner corpus research: A methodological synthesis
records.summary: Longitudinal learner corpus research (LCR) has grown substantially in recent years, resulting in richness and variety in study designs, analyses, and findings. Yet its design, measurement, and analysis practices have not been systematically assessed. To address this gap, this review synthesizes 120 longitudinal learner corpus studies published between 1996 and 2025, identified through systematic database searches and supplementary searching of the Learner Corpus Bibliography. records.summary: Human language comprehension is remarkably robust---we are good at grasping what speakers and writers intend and can even understand them when their productions are not perfectly well-formed. records.title: Color Vision for Human Factors Engineering: When Color Helps, When It Hurts, and for Whom
records.summary: Color vision serves everyday tasks, from judging food and reading skin to segmenting scenes and reading signs, displays, and data. Designers use color in safety codes, interfaces, visualizations, lighting, and interiors, but practice often outruns evidence. I review when color helps, when it hurts, and for whom. records.summary: Ensuring equitable language learning support for everyone has become an urgent necessity, considering increasingly linguistically diverse classrooms. Understanding how linguistic backgrounds affect language learning outcomes is crucial, beyond the binary categories of non-native vs. native. Linguistic distance (LD) measures present more nuanced instruments to investigate the effect of the speaker's mother tongue. records.summary: Purpose: The development of reading fluency relies on phonological skills and prosodic competence, but evidence about the developmental mechanisms underlying this relationship remain scarce. records.title: The Structure and Content of Meaning in Speech Reflects Mental Health
records.summary: Mental health shapes the progression and content of thought. Studies have linked depression, anxiety, and stress with repetitive negative thoughts, but it remains unclear whether these disturbances are reflected in the structure of an individual's speech. We introduce an approach to quantify the structure of thought as expressed in language, applying it to memory recountings from 82 individuals across six psychotherapy sessions. records.summary: This study investigates how information congruency influences memory during sentence comprehension. Although previous research has shown that congruent information facilitates comprehension, it remains unclear whether this advantage arises already at the earliest stages of memory encoding. records.summary: How many languages does a person speak? This study examines blame attribution in the Danish Parliament from 1997 to 2026, combining a purpose-built classifier, BlameBERT (F1: 0.80), with multilevel statistical modeling. The classifier is constructed using an annotation-efficient pipeline for blame attribution in low-to-mid resource languages. records.summary: Emotional speech is an important carrier of affective information in spoken communication. Its perception depends on the joint processing of emotional semantics and prosody, yet the relative contribution of these two information sources varies across individuals and contexts. However, a unified account is still lacking of why their processing weights change and how the brain dynamically adjusts them according to the reliability of incoming information. records.title: Beyond problem solving: Adaptive reframing in human and artificial intelligence
records.summary: Research on human and artificial intelligence has largely focused on problem solving: given a predefined problem, can an agent produce an effective solution? Yet many real-world challenges cannot be captured by a fixed problem representation. They require agents not only to solve problems, but also to recognize when the original problem representation has become inadequate and must be revised to reflect new evidence or changes in the problem itself. records.summary: Frame Semantics offers a compelling framework for representing meaning as structured conceptual scenarios (frames). FrameNet operationalizes this theory as a lexical resource linking words to frames and their conceptual roles (frame elements, FEs). records.summary: Affective valence is widely regarded as a core organizing dimension in word recognition, yet findings on its role remain inconsistent. We argue that this inconsistency reflects a longstanding operationalization of valence as a domain-general signal. records.title: English-learning infants’ perception of word stress patterns
records.summary: Adult speakers of different free stress languages (e.g., English, Spanish) differ both in their sensitivity to lexical stress and in their processing of suprasegmental and vowel quality cues to stress. In a head-turn preference experiment with a familiarization phase, both 8-month-old and 12-month-old English-learning infants discriminated between initial stress and final stress among lists of Spanish-spoken disyllabic nonwords that were segmentally varied (e.g., [ˈnila, ˈtuli] vs. [luˈta, puˈki]). This is evidence that English-learning infants are sensitive to lexical stress patterns, instantiated primarily by suprasegmental cues, during the second half of the first year of life.

records.summary: Audio-recordings collected with a child-worn device are a fundamental tool in child language research. Long-form recordings collected over whole days promise to capture children’s input and production with minimal observer bias, and therefore high validity. The sheer volume of resulting data necessitates automated analysis to extract relevant metrics for researchers and clinicians. This paper summarizes collective knowledge on this technique, providing entry points to existing resources. records.summary: Part of language development necessarily involves connecting sensory input with linguistic units. records.summary: A widely accepted framework in multilingual control is the inhibitory control model (ICM, Green, 1998). records.summary: Recent research has shown individual differences in gradiency, defined as sensitivity to fine-grained acoustic differences at the subphonemic level. records.summary: Semantic network analyses have shown that words in spoken languages are organized into efficient "small-world" structures that support rapid lexical access and retrieval. records.summary: Language and emotion are closely interconnected, with words carrying affective properties, such as emotional valence, ranging from negative to positive with a neutral midpoint, and emotional polarity, which reflects the absolute distance from that midpoint. records.summary: Rule generalization is one of the most useful tools our mind uses to facilitate learning. records.summary: This study focuses on parental language beliefs, which we approach from an attitudes perspective. records.title: Infants’ learning of tones and VOT contrasts in the lab
records.summary: Infants likely home in on the speech categories in the ambient language(s) by attending to the acoustic cue distributions present in the input, but direct experimental evidence for this remains scarce.
